utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I'm able to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Good morning to you, and you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, also good morning to my learned friends for the Defence. I am here with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I represent Mr. Naser Oric. With us is our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, last Thursday or Friday I was informed by one of my staff members that -- and I was also handed a copy of the joint letter that you sent that more or less you have reached some sort of agreement or you're confident that you will reach one as regards mutual -- as regards disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So can we bring in the witness, please, Mr. -- or Dr. Eric Dachy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Dr. Dachy. Good morning to you, Dr. Dachy, and welcome to this Tribunal. You're being summoned as a witness for the Defence in this trial against Naser Oric. Very soon you will commence with your testimony. Our Rules require that before you do so you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath to the extent -- in the sense that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained on the piece of paper which is being handed to you now by Madam Usher. Please read it out loud and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Dr. Dachy. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have -- is it you, Mr. Jones, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones will be putting to you a set of questions and he will then be followed by Mr. Di Fazio for the Prosecution. Is it your first time in a courtroom, Dr. Dachy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such as this court, yes. I was a witness as a child in a courtroom in Belgium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. More or less the procedure is pretty much similar to what it is in most domestic jurisdictions. So you will be asked questions. Please try to answer the question in as -- a concise way but as fully as possible and to the best of your ability. And if you have any problems at any time with interpretation, please draw your attention straight away so that we rectify the problem. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you please give the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: My name is Eric Dachy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: 1st of March, 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your nationality, please?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: I'm a Belgian national.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that you currently live in Brussels?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, well in the suburbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you're a medical doctor by training?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a medical doctor. I have been a doctor since 1988. Presently I'm doing a specialty in child psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I don't think it's in dispute. You first joined (redacted) in 1991 to work in Kurdistan. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in October 1991 you took a job as head of mission for (redacted) in the former Yugoslavia, based in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: In 1991. It was still Yugoslavia then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that your job was to define and implement programmes for(redacted)?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. As the head of mission, my task was -- or my responsibility was absolute as to everything that was done in the area. And of course my role was to obtain the authorisation and the support of our headquarters in Brussels, Paris, and Amsterdam.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that you had (redacted) branches in Zagreb and Sarajevo, both of which reported to you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As part of your work did you visit places, and if so what type of places?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, constantly. Of course my work was first and foremost to be as best-informed as I could as to what was really happening on the ground. Therefore, when I arrived in October the place that was the main focus was of course the city of Vukovar, and some of the refugees who had fled from the war areas in Croatia or Serbia. So the first places I went to were really taking most of our attention, as that was the front line around Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to ask you briefly about Vukovar, but just very briefly. But firstly, are you familiar with the book "War Hospital" by Sheri Fink?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I met the author or the author met me on several occasions in order to interview me. She asked me to proofread the book. So I corrected the book and I also gave her the written notes that I had kept from my stay in the Balkans. So, yes, I'm very familiar with the contents of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, that book sets out, among other things, your experiences in Vukovar when the town was besieged and then fell to Serb forces. I'm not going to ask you about Vukovar in any detail except to ask you this: Do you see any relevance in what you observed in Vukovar in terms of what you later saw in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, I do because Vukovar to me was a hallucinating experience because of what I saw. I had flown into Belgrade on a regular airline, and I took a taxi as you take taxis anywhere in the world to go up to the front line. And I discovered there was an army with scores of guns, cannons, busy destroying a city. And I said that I was a doctor and I said so in order to go to the medical services near the front line, and I happened to discover in what condition the people were who left the city. And it was really horrible; the people were traumatised. They had been wounded by snipers, by shrapnel, or had just hid for weeks on end in their cellars. They didn't even dare to go out to try and get some water. And you could understand that in the city it was a whole deluge of fire constantly day and night. So I saw children who were totally catatonic. They couldn't say a word anymore because they were so terrorised. Everything was happening day after day, hour after hour, week after week, and it was literally the destruction of a city. It was truly something that was incomprehensible to any European who would have been there. Later on I understood that this was actually a well-established military strategy, which was to besiege a town, to isolate the town first, to encircle it, and then to reduce its defence to nothing through artillery. But when I say "artillery" it is a systematic deluge of shells falling on every square metre of the town, and then starting with street warfare, street fights with these very famous paramilitary units, which I saw on many occasions around Vukovar when we would go and sort of visit around to explore the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when you refer to that well-established military strategy, is that something which you observed subsequently in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. What I saw in Vukovar was that indeed there was heavy artillery attacking a defenceless town, there were special units of those who were already called the Chetniks, those ultra-nationalist Serbs. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. They really looked wild. You could see them coming back from the front line with bloody knives, with obscene laughter, with behaviour that was openly boisterous and joyful, while obviously this was a context of atrocity. And then these people would take the town and there would be executions. Because in Vukovar, as I was allowed to enter the city as soon as it was taken, I went to the hospital. And together with the International Red Cross representative, I could see and he was quite upset, all the males -- the male patients had been taken. Although we thought -- it was confirmed later on, these male patients were executed a bit further out. So these are the three ingredients that I saw in Vukovar, ingredients that I found first in Bijeljina again, it is a small town in the north of Bosnia. The Bosnian Serbs took that little town, ruled it in the same way, whilst we would regularly go to Bosnia and try to keep abreast of the places where people might need help at a given point in time. The entire area of Bijeljina was just forbidden; we couldn't access it. And we knew that there was a lot of gunfire to be heard and then it was sort of blackout. We couldn't hear a thing or know a thing, and I would insist to be authorised to get to Bijeljina. And the same way it happened in Vukovar, I was able to enter the town with our team. And we could see -- it was obvious that Arkan's men, the head of this Serb paramilitary unit, had taken the city. And we heard that people were killed -- had been killed, and that the Serbs took over power very violently. And I suspected that there was a lot of casualties, fatalities, the first thing I did was to go to hospital --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because I'm going to come to Bijeljina shortly. Just before we leave Vukovar I just wanted to present a map so we can find Vukovar and some other places in relation to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We've got copies of the map for everyone. Just for the record it's "Extract of a Map of the Military Geographical Institute" from 1967 and the scale is 1:1.500.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I use this opportunity to ask you whether I'm speaking too fast?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you'll see on the ELMO to your right, Dr. Dachy, in a moment anyway -- well, you can see in any event the map. And I'm going to ask you -- I'm going to ask you just if you could locate Vukovar and also Sarajevo and Srebrenica and circle each of them.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. Vukovar is a small town on the Danube River about one and a half hours drive from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just for the record, that's in Croatia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes -- well, it's really on the border because the Danube is the border between Serbia and Croatia -- well, at least at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you would also circle Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Sarajevo, we would go there very often, driving from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you could circle Srebrenica, please.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that when you were in the Vukovar region you saw soldiers or paramilitaries returning from the front. Where was that, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: There were two places we could access close to the front line. The first place was Sid, a small town which can be found here on this map. It's a bit further away from Sid but it is on the territory. And then there was another location north of Vukovar, close to Borovo Naselje which can't be seen here, and you could get there from the north. I'm showing you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: In dotted lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could initial the map and then I would ask for that to be tendered as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think it should be D707.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 707.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this map which has been initialled by the witness is being tendered and received and marked as Defence exhibit D707.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, leaving Vukovar, when did you first become aware that war had broken out or was breaking out in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: The exact time when we knew that the war had broken out, that's sort of around the 6th or the 8th of April officially, when there was this big demonstration in Sarajevo. But in practice, on the ground as we saw it in Bijeljina, the war had already started. There was this big demonstration in Sarajevo; I followed that on TV. It was actually eventually aimed at preventing this war which had started or was starting. But when this demonstration found a tragic end because strivers [as interpreted] shot some protesters, demonstrators, everybody understood that unfortunately so the war had really started for good and nobody could prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Bijeljina and a little bit of what you saw there. Where in fact did you go when you went to Bijeljina and when did you go there? If you can help us with that.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Throughout this period from February to April, we of course tried to realise to what extent help or aid was -- medical aid was necessary in some places because of fighting and because people were isolated and to see where an international organisation could have done some useful work. But it was really difficult to assess -- ascertain where these people -- these places were if you didn't go yourself on the ground. And this way we became aware - also through information I was able to gather indirectly - I became aware that the Bijeljina area was a city we had gone through or we would go through because it was on the road to Sarajevo and also on the way to several other Bosnian towns when you go to Bosnia through that way. So Bijeljina was a place that we would know very well because we had gone through it, which was quite normal until it was totally isolated. And after the Arkan's militia has conquered it, it was difficult to access it. When I was able to go with me team to the city after it had been taken by the Serbs, I went to the hospital. Do you want me to explain what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps if you can give a precis or summary of some of the things you observed in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Clearly when we entered Bijeljina in the town there were a lot of adult men on street corners, in small groups of five to ten. Most of them were on street corners; that was systematic. And when we got into the town, we were escorted by a Serbian military car and we -- there was a time when we had to slow down at traffic lights, so we tried to ask people -- those people what they were doing there. And they said, We're here and we want to show that we are peaceful, that we're not armed. Obviously these people were afraid and we understood that following the fighting, these were Bosnian people who wanted to show that they were not fighters, warmongers. We went straight away to the hospital where I met the head, director of the hospital, a Bosnian woman. She looked very afraid and she often asked me whether I wanted to see the morgue. I didn't want to because it was not my role. I wanted precisely to avoid being involved in things that could be seen in a bad light, and our priority was to provide aid. But she also wanted to make me understand that there had been a lot of people being killed during the fighting, during the takeover of the city. While she was talking to me she was violently replaced [as interpreted] whilst I was there in front of my eyes by a new director of the hospital, a Serb man, who behaved quite violently who just sort of dismissed her. He sat down and said, I am the new director, do you have questions? Then he lectured me, gave me a political lecture on the dangers that the Bosnian Muslims were, the fact that now freedom had been re-established in Bijeljina. So I didn't harbour much illusion as to what that meant. I understood that the town was in the hands of the Serbs, that it would be a very intransigent type of takeover and later we learned from the High Commissioner for Refugees that all the men had been deported.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One interpretation issue. I think at least once anyway you referred to Bosniak and it was translated as Bosnian. Provided it's understood that of course Bosniak means Bosnian Muslim, is it correct that when you're referring to Bosniak you're referring to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. If we say "Muslims" in the sense of nationality, such as it was established in Yugoslavia, the majority of people that I met and who claimed Bosniak identity were laymen but who asserted their Bosniak identity. They may have been descendents of people who converted to Islam but who no longer claimed Muslim identity but rather Bosniak. And for me this was important because there were many people that the Serbs called "Turks" or "Muslims" who were simply people who were discriminated against because they had names that had Ottoman connections but who were Bosniaks. So if you don't mind, I will continue to refer to them as Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, just so it's clear for the record. I want to ask you just very briefly about Zvornik. Did you go to Zvornik in this period?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because I want to take it quite briefly. Can you tell us when you went to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: According to the best of my memory, it was just after the war Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. officially broke out, that is after the period of the 6th to the 8th of April. And we went to Bijeljina just before that, the last days of March or the very beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was what you saw in Zvornik a similar -- similar events to what you saw in Bijeljina or was it in any way different?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: In Zvornik, in my view, it was exactly the same pattern that we saw, the isolation of the town, then a siege, artillery fire, and then the conquest of the town by special units. But we arrived at a slightly different moment. That is, we were not aware that we were going to such dangerous places that people were fleeing. So we arrived at Zvornik just when the town was being taken over; it was not under military control. We arrived when there was still street fighting in Zvornik, and there was a lot of shots fired around us. And when we reached the hospital, the situation was still rather uncertain. And rather like Bijeljina, we were able to meet the staff, the hospital director, who were mostly Bosniaks but there were also Serbs. They were very nice. They were afraid. And when we were discussing the situation, we were interrupted by the arrival of special troops, the leader of which, we learned later, was known under the name of Commander Marko. Commander Marko and his men were extremely threatening. They wanted to arrest our driver and interpreter; we opposed this. And they were extremely brutal. They told us to shut up, that we had nothing to say, and eventually they questioned us about what we were doing, and they didn't really believe -- they finally believed what we were saying and they let us go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, as part of your work did you speak to many Bosniak refugees from Bijeljina, Zvornik, and other places in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: On that day leaving Zvornik we saw a column of people on the road who were going towards Serbia. There were women, children, the elderly. We took them in our vehicle to help them reach the place where they could take a bus. And we spoke to them. We asked them what was happening, and they described the pattern that I just described, that is that the town was isolated, one couldn't move around, it became dangerous, there were shells and snipers until the takeover was complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did these stories circulate among refugees, what had happened in these various towns?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The people around Zvornik told us, and in Serbia itself we also had work to do, and that is to provide aid to small refugee centres where the people had found shelter. These used to be holiday homes for children with 30 to 50 places which took in families from Bosnia, from Croatia. And we went to visit those people. But the refugees in Serbia were very cautious about what they were going to say because they depended directly on the communal authorities, the local authorities, for the aid they received. And it was their interest to demonstrate that they were good citizens, or rather good and faithful inhabitants. So they would not disclose any details that were not in line with the official policies and theories in Krajina and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move to Srebrenica now and ask you when you first heard about Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: In this period, that is the spring of 1992, our aim was to try and find out, as I said, to what extent -- what was happening and where people needed aid urgently. And this was difficult because of the large territory. They may have needed medical aid, food, or any other kind of aid. There were people fleeing through the woods. There were stories of women delivering in the fields. And it was very difficult to obtain information. And the front line was something that we were not informed about directly because this was under military control. So I informed myself through correspondence of international agencies, I attended meetings, coordination meetings, of UN bodies like the High Commissioner for Refugees representatives, and so on. And we knew that in Bosnia, in Eastern Bosnia, that there was quite violent combat, as the Serbs wanted to dominate it -- this area. And names cropped up frequently to the effect that there was an area where people had grouped together and were isolated. And this area had a name. It was Srebrenica. And we were told that resistance in Zvornik and Bijeljina and in other places was very weak, those perhaps people fought bravely, but it was clear that they were not up to the level of the forces that could be deployed by the Serbs. And in this area of Bosnia and Srebrenica, there was resistance. And the name given to that resistance was "Naser Oric." This is a name that cropped up at that time already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you when you first entered Srebrenica, when you first actually physically went there?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: When people spoke of the area, I gathered that there were people there who needed aid because they were isolated by the war. And it was in places like that that urgent humanitarian aid had meaning. And immediately we told ourselves, not just me but other organisations as well, that we had to go there. To reach Srebrenica, I negotiated with the Serbian Republic of Bosnia, which had a sort of embassy in Belgrade. I had met Radovan Karadzic once to ask him for permission to intervene in Bosnia. And we understood as soon as we said that we wanted to go to Srebrenica that it was useless to even mention that name, that we would never get permission to go there. They refused access to Bosnia by aid organisations and it was hopeless. So I tried to encourage and to rely on the UN, the High Commissioner for Refugees that had links with UNPROFOR so that diplomatic pressure should result in our accessing Srebrenica, and that is what indeed happened. The UN managed to obtain permission to send a convoy to Srebrenica. I was able to take a place -- to get on the second convoy that was going to Srebrenica, and that was on the 4th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you describe what it was like arriving there, what you observed when you arrived on the 4th of December, 1992, what the conditions were like.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: We were familiar with Bosnia. We knew the roads to be able to conduct our aid operations. And reaching Srebrenica, I was with another doctor, the director of the MF [as interpreted] at the time, and an interpreter. And we covered the few kilometres from Bratunac to Srebrenica via Potocari, and we left the armoured vehicle. And we were all astonished because we had reached another world. This small town was visibly damaged. There were crowds everywhere. Though it was December, it was still sunny and it was more like an autumn day, a sunny day, but the people were sad, without hope, desperate, dirty, greyish, dusty, and glad to see us but also extremely anxious. The town -- or rather, the area around it was exposed to shell fire and we were immediately hit by this feeling of physical and psychological misery, which was reflected in the clothing, in the behaviour, the attitude of the people we encountered. And as we knew that we would not be staying long, we focussed on the hospital, and that was where we stopped. The hospital was across the way -- across the road from the PTT building --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there for a moment. It's a question of something that might have been left out in translation. Before you said "desesperes." Then you said "emacies." Did you use that word, that the people were emaciated?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones, that will show up in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But an obvious question: For what reason in your opinion were they emaciated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he needs to mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned going to the hospital. Did you meet anyone at the hospital? Did anyone receive you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: When one in a humanitarian worker, one has to respect the formal system. So we didn't rush into the hospital as if we had the right to go to a hospital without asking anyone, but rather we asked to see the officials responsible for the hospital. And they asked us were kindly to wait for a few minutes, which we did. And then Dr. Mujkanovic arrived, who was the most responsible official.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right that you came to know Dr. Mujkanovic over the coming months?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. The time I spent with him was so important -- the moments I spent with him were so important. One realised who one was dealing with, and the situation in Srebrenica was so intense from many points of view that they had a very impressive look. And Dr. Mujkanovic was clearly a person of great importance at the beginning of the events in Srebrenica. At first, I met him very briefly. I saw him later, but clearly he was playing an important role and he was an impressive personality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he tell you about the work he had been doing in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. That was our main question: The medical situation in the hospital. Because obviously we wanted to know what needed to be done in terms of medical aid to the population, because though we knew they needed food as well, our main focus was on medical aid. And the situation there was again quite extraordinary. Nedret told us of the conditions he was working in, the extremely difficult conditions, that he lacked instruments and bandages and everything -- that everything was quite dirty, though they tried to clean things as best they could. But they didn't have the means to sterilise, and we realised that these conditions were absolutely unimaginable. And he took us around the hospital rooms where we saw people in an abominable conditions. It is the only thing one can say about it. He had absolutely nothing to treat Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. anyone with. There wasn't a drop of disinfectant. There wasn't a single roll of bandage. There wasn't a millilitre of aspirins or antibiotics or anything at all. So there was no aid he could give to any of the wounded. There was one example, a little girl who was crying in her bed. I assume she was there because she was alone otherwise she would be at home. She had a broken arm because she had fallen from a tree, and two small branches had been attached and some sticky paper had been put round those two twigs to keep the arm in place, but this had absolutely no effect. There was nothing that could be done in that way and it was miserable and pathetic at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll come back and ask you a specific question or two about that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have a short video clip which we want to show for a couple of purposes. One of them is identification of Dr. Mujkanovic, if possible, by this witness. I should explain that it was -- it's been suggested by another witness that maybe Dr. Mujkanovic wasn't actually engaged in medicine, so it's partly for that purpose. It's also for the purposes of identifying someone else in the clip and also for just showing how abominable the conditions were, because we say that's relevant to questions of control priorities. It's pretty grisly. It will be ten seconds or so, or maybe a bit longer. And with your permission I'll show that briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from -- this I understand is an amputation scene, isn't it, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection on your part? We don't have a jury so -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not concerned about that aspect. I make that absolutely plain. I'm not concerned about that in the slightest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not going to be impressed in any case. MR. DI FAZIO: It's not that. But what is the point of this? I mean, there's no dispute that Mujkanovic must have attended the hospital on occasions and Dr. Dachy can tell us all about that, number one. Number two -- and I understand what Mr. Jones is saying about the evidence of the other gentleman who spoke about him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't need to go into that. MR. DI FAZIO: So we don't need to go into that. So it's not really going to assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the last witness we are going to hear on these events basically, so -- MR. DI FAZIO: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: After this witness, we are not going to hear it. MR. DI FAZIO: All I'm saying is I don't think it will advance the case to see an amputation, but if you must.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope this has proved well enough the futility of the whole exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond, it is important to show that Dr. Mujkanovic did on occasion drop into the hospital --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't think the Trial Chamber would doubt for a moment that Dr. Mujkanovic was there working under the conditions that Dr. Dachy has been --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the second submission, and it is part of our case, that Srebrenica was a chamber of horrors at the time, that that has a major bearing on what priorities were, whether one should investigate vandalism to properties or whether one should avoid these sorts of casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I told you go ahead, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- be quite brief. If you can see the screen, Dr. Dachy, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we are not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The third one. Yes. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- if you can identify anyone or see anything about the images.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you tell us when to stop, Mr. Dachy, yourself, please. Or when you would like to put questions to him, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'll perhaps pause at one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do whichever way is more convenient to you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, if you can provide any commentary, Dr. Dachy, if you recognise anyone or if you can say whether this is a surgery that you saw in the hospital, any reflections.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: No, no, I can see that indeed the person is not even on a proper table like for surgery. He's just on a stretcher. Yes, I can see some that -- one of the rooms where surgery was done in the hospital because you have to know that it was just sort of a medical centre with some beds. There was no proper operating theatre. So this is all improvised. You don't have any sterile conditions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you recognise any of the doctors there, the one in green or any of those in white, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Right. I can see that the instruments used are totally ill-adapted. They do what they can with what they have. I fail to recognise these two people in white coats on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... few seconds, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Only if you're able to, are you able to identify the man in --

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: No, I really am not sure that I recognise Nedret here. I can't identify him in a -- with any degree of certainty on this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We'll carry on a bit further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This lady we've just seen passing by is one of doctors [as interpreted] -- I think she was a Croat by origin. And then the man -- the doctor with a beard is Ilijas Pilav. One of the people you saw in the background, yes, I recognise that person but I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Stop that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you in fact - I'm skipping forward a bit - at one point perform an operation with Dr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. When we came back the second time, that was in March 1993 after that winter in Srebrenica when we came back. That was together with General Morillon this time. We again focussed on the hospital. Nedret asked one of us to help him because somebody had been wounded with shrapnel in the abdomen some hours before. So I helped him perform surgery. It took at least four to five hours, and in the same conditions as the one we've just seen. So absolutely no hygiene -- well, we had some gloves because we had brought some medical supplies with us. And earlier on you asked me about Nedret. It was really quite a lesson in bravery, in courage, because if I can talk medically for a while. This person had been hurt through a shall hole in the abdomen area through some shrapnel. And the problem was that it was a tiny hole but that the shrapnel is going to perforate the intestine in the bowel. You can't live with that because it's a source of infection. So the surgeon has to open and close the bowel everywhere where it was perforated. It has to find this shrapnel, if possible. So this is a long and difficult type of work and the search is of bowel tissue and very inefficient, and the prognosis very bad in -- even in a good hospital. So this type of work was doomed to failure, I thought. And it was really hard not to lose courage before, especially in these conditions, before you started I mean. But at the same time, you couldn't let this man die just like that. We couldn't kill him ourselves either; he was screaming with pain. So Nedret operated on him. And I was obviously quite heartless. I wasn't saying a word, of course, but I found it hard to believe in what we were doing and at the same time I was afraid and I lost heart. He must have felt it, Nedret, because at some point somebody came into the room, somebody quite joyful, somebody who was quite loud speaking in Bosnian. Nedret said something to that person. He came close to me and opened his shirt and showed a huge scar that he had, really big one, and a very ugly scar on his belly, and Nedret said he had the same except and I operated on him without any anaesthetic. Because this time we had used Ketamine which is some kind of anaesthetic that is not quite enough but it does lessen the pain. So I understood that he was really doing wonders. The man said, Nedret, good doctor, and he left happy, obviously glad to be alive in spite of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to move on to March 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones. Who shot these scenes? Who made this video?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Someone who is going to be a witness, Mustafa Sacirovic. I'm going to start with some short questions and if you could just give some short answers to those -- to some specific issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, what was Dr. Mujkanovic wearing when you met him in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: The very first time when he came to see us he was in complete Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. uniform with a badge from Bosnia-Herzegovina. On top of that he had sunglasses, a cap, a beret, so he looked like a soldier rather than a hospital director, so my first reflex was to be a little bit frightened because I thought, God, this is a very militarised situation. But as soon as I got to know him I understood that he was simply a true surgeon and that he'd been sent from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know where he got that uniform from?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: No idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you see anyone else on that day, December 1992 -- Bosniaks I mean, not internationals -- in uniform?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: No, I didn't. When we crossed the checkpoint close to Potocari, this sort of entry into Bosnian territory in Srebrenica, there were a few soldiers but they had pieces of uniforms, nothing matching. They were trying to identify themselves as fighters, but it was mainly the weapon that would show that they were fighters. They had absolutely no uniform, nothing that looked like a standard uniform, absolutely nothing of the kind. There were sort of all parts of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we move on to your visit in March of 1993, you did comment on this girl with her arm fixed to tree branches with Scotch tape. I just want you to comment, if you can, how in your opinion the conditions of life in Srebrenica at that time impacted on the ability to show initiative and to find solutions to problems.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, when I saw this little girl, it was a very disturbing sight. If we had just taken the trouble of getting some pieces of wood, of really cutting them well and to try to put them around her arm, even with an old piece of cloth, it was possible to hold the arm in a better way than had been done. I saw two or three other cases of wounded people. I saw a lady whose femur was broken and her leg had not at all been put in a traction, like in a better holding, just they used some rope and some pieces of wood. I realised that the medical team had somehow given up, but it was our job as humanitarian workers to really understand the situation. It was ruled out to blame the team, of course. This -- the team needed help themselves because if you are a doctor and you feel powerless, doomed to be powerless with no means to react in face -- in the face of people who were weakened, ill day after day, it is a very traumatising situation. So we sort of agreed among ourselves because we were quite moved and outraged by the condition of the wounded. We had the feeling that the team were passive, but at the same time, simultaneously, due to our experience we had this reflex. We thought that this led us to understand how serious the situation was. This was an indicia of desperation, hopelessness, of how critical the situation was. They were absolutely saturated. They were burned out, as they say. They were unable to react, even in the cases where they could have used the means that they had. So Nedret was, therefore, very impressive because he never gave up. It may have happened a couple of times --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll stop you there to keep your answers a bit shorter. That burnout which you describe, would that apply only to the hospital or is that something which you would apply generally to the situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, outside it looked even worse than in the hospital because in the hospital -- well, there were people in uniforms and I understood that all those working in the hospital would get some food at least for being there. So there was still some degree of structure there, but outside it was total chaos, indescribable, it was total hopelessness, despair. You could feel that everybody in the city was doomed to be tragically powerless because at the same time there was this terrible threat of military aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I also want to deal briefly with your trip in -- into and out of Srebrenica through Bratunac. What were the reactions of local Serbs to your visit to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: You mean in December?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Well, in December it was particularly difficult to reach -- to get in because the local authorities in Bratunac, including the military from the Bosnian Serb army who were very present -- I mean they were omnipresent in the area, they just wouldn't let us go through in spite of the good papers that we had, that had been produced by the UN people in charge who were in the convoy. So obviously the people were very much against the idea of aid reaching the inhabitants of Srebrenica. And Radovan Karadzic had to come by helicopter for us to be able to cross the roadblocks from the Serb military in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the Bosnian Serb army was omnipresent in the area. Would you agree or disagree with the description of this area as being militarised? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please, I object to that question unless there's a basis for his knowledge. So far the witness has described travelling from Bratunac into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Srebrenica. MR. DI FAZIO: Srebrenica, remaining in Srebrenica, and I assume travelling out with a convoy, a humanitarian convoy, and his exit. And again, I assume -- it may be wrong, Mr. Jones can lead him on this, but I assume the same pattern occurred in March. Now, unless he toured the area and was able to tour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed, agreed, Mr. Di Fazio. Yes. I think that describes the objection, which can only be sustained in that context --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you can limit your question to the zone, the particular area travelled by the witness, yes, okay, go ahead. Otherwise please don't extend it to include an area which maybe the witness doesn't really understand what that -- it covers more than he actually saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I think two points, Your Honour. Firstly I could ask the witness to explain what he means by "in the area," because otherwise it's not clear, and secondly ask him where else in this area he travelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So first when you say the Bosnian Serb army was omnipresent in the area, what area are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Well, yes, I'm talking about the whole area controlled by the Serbs. And little by little we discovered that it was under Serb control. So from spring of 1992 we were trying to carry out exploratory missions but also aid-providing missions everywhere where we could access the area. So we did travel a lot around Bosnia in that time, for instance by setting up an assistance programme to hospitals -- to the Serbian hospitals in Bosnia. So we could go everywhere where it was needed. Of course we had to get permits, we had to cross roadblocks, and we had set up an aid programme to a psychiatric hospital that had been totally abandoned near Modrica, Koprivnak [phoen] on this northern corridor, as it was called. So we were familiar with this area. I may not have gone personally on every trip, but I received reports from my teams who were circulating around because we had to agree when -- about security problems, for instance. So this was the area under Serb control and we would go around as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, ever encounter Serb -- the Serb military close up? Did you see at close range artillery or tanks or APCs?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: All the time. For instance, when we would take the road to Modrica through Brcko, which Banja Luka -- we were very close to the rears of the front line. We would cross the front line on some spots. It was rare to have very visible pieces of artillery, but you would hear them because you could hear the shots and you see people on guard. All the towns or the roads or the areas that had been taken over in a stable way by the Serbs were run by the Bosnian Serb army. So it -- we always had to deal with officers, non-commissioned officers when we would go around, when we had to sleep somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And specifically dealing with the Srebrenica area, did you travel along the Drina much in this period, late 1992/early 1993?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: We tried to, but it was forbidden, even in Serbia. The police would not let you go down that road, only exceptionally so, that is go on the Serbian side on the Drina. We couldn't go further down than Mali Zvornik, which is the city opposite Zvornik. We could not go to Bratunac or to Ljubovija which is across from Bratunac. We were not allowed to go further down. It was possible to access these areas by going through inner Serbia, going through Uzice and the mountains, but it's quite a way out. So we had no real reason to go there. Our idea was more to go through Bosnia and the authorised crossing was Zvornik, Mali Zvornik, and Zvornik. So it was better to use that crossing rather than go around even if we tried to do so a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were there ever -- did you ever see anything which actually would declare, signs for example, that an area was a war zone? Is that something which you saw?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: You mean in Bosnia or in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. First of all, if you want to get into Bosnia just to cross that bridge and reach the Bosnian bank of the Drina, usually you had a major military checkpoint. You needed to have a written permit to enter Bosnia, a permit that was delivered by -- well, I call this the embassy, but it was the representative of what was so-called the Serb Republic of Bosnia in Belgrade. It was the former Bosnian republic villa in Belgrade. Obviously you were reaching an area under military control and you needed a special permit. And generally when you had it, it was checked by telephone, you know, somewhere with a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. headquarters. And then of course you had boards where it was written "ratna zona." It was not at the very entry of Bosnia, but these were boards showing civilians, whether they -- civilian Serbs, local Serbs, they were not to go any further, that it was dangerous because it was an area with military activity and it was clearly indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And sorry if I appeared to cut you short sometimes, but I need to explore certain of your answers. You referred to crossing that bridge. Which bridge would that refer to?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb authorities demanded that the crossing to Bosnia be the bridge linking Bosnia and Serbia in Zvornik, and its equivalent, Mali Zvornik, which is that small village in Serbia. So this is the place where all humanitarian convoys to Bosnia and UNPROFOR convoys as well as Red Cross convoys were supposed to go through. And that's where they waited for authorisations. Sometimes there were hundreds of trucks waiting for the goodwill of the Serb authorities just to go -- to cross that bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you cross the bridge ever from Ljubovija to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. That bridge is the one we used in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you -- sorry, I do need to keep it short. And was authorisation required to cross that bridge or not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Let's say that, yes, it was certainly required, but in this respect we left it to the UN. We gave the UNHCR our whereabouts, translations of our identity papers, the contents of the trucks, the number plates, but it was the UN who would take care of getting authorisations to go to Srebrenica in every station of the journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then finally, just dealing with Bratunac, can you describe for us briefly what you saw in terms of Serb military presence in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: This is a biggish town, it's spread out, under total military control it was at the time. The military were omnipresent. We knew that we were close to the front line. We could hear guns firing, and I think that economic activity -- I mean that at the time was rather reduced. It was very quiet, rather deserted. But there was still some civilian population; the people were very hostile to international presence. That was true in Ljubovija. Children would do death signs to us. Everybody was blaming us with helping the enemy, and we would be stopped by military or arrested even. We were kept one night in Ljubovija because we had been detained the night before. So only the day after when Radovan Karadzic came by helicopter and went to negotiate with his own troops, only then were we allowed to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. And before the break I'll just ask you: Did you return to Srebrenica? And if so, on what date?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: I returned -- well, I went during the war in December in 1992 and in March 1993, and I returned to Srebrenica I believe 1998, 1998. I passed through the city in a car, but I didn't want to stay. I saw the buildings and then I went away. It was very sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And -- yes, after the break I'm going to ask about your visit in March of 1993. It's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Dr. Dachy, there's no dispute that on the 11st of March, 1993, you returned to Srebrenica with General Morillon and his team. Were you obstructed at all on your return to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On his return or on the way to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On the way to Srebrenica. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. May I explain the circumstances of this trip to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, of course, briefly.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: We waited 11 days in front of the bridge to be able to enter Srebrenica. There were dozens of persons, officials of the United Nations like Hollingworth, dozens of trucks, a convoy waiting to be able to cross the bridge between Mali Zvornik and Zvornik. So I don't know whether you can imagine what it meant to wait 11 days for permission to cross. We were finally able to enter Srebrenica because General Morillon had visited Konjevic Polje. He stayed in a motel in Banja Koviljaca. He held a press conference saying, I will go to Srebrenica. We are leaving tomorrow morning. And he said that the Serbs had agreed. And the next day, we followed General Morillon. It was a question of maximum diplomatic pressure that enabled us to go to Srebrenica. I think that the number two from UNPROFOR, the head of UNPROFOR in Bosnia had decided that there was agreement by the Serbs, and we went there. Clearly the trip was not as simple as he had imagined. Do you wish me to describe the trip or would that take too much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to take it by stages with specific questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just one question to clarify. When you speak we returned or you returned to Srebrenica with Morillon, does that mean that you were part of the convoy of General Morillon or on the occasion of General Morillon entering Srebrenica you also were joining the whole affair so to say? Have you been part of the convoy of General Morillon or somehow joining him as a separate group, so to say? And if you speak about problems, do you refer to your own group or to the whole convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question. Clearly, we were part of General Morillon's group as (redacted) and we asked publicly whether he would agree to take doctors with him and an interpreter. So we were part of the group. And as I explained previously, this was our only chance to reach places that were difficult to get access to. And we relied on the UN agencies for negotiations. And when General Morillon said, I'm going to Srebrenica, I asked also, Can you take us with you? And he said (redacted) were welcome. And basically the convoy consisted of UNPROFOR members, members of the UNHCR, and three doctors of (redacted) as interpreted]. Furthermore, as we needed to prepare a minimum convoy of urgent necessities, General Morillon decided that we would pass through with a single truck, and we filled half of this truck with medical material which we assumed was urgently needed. And UNHCR and UNPROFOR said that the other half of the truck should be filled with sugar, which was obviously equally important. So there was one truck consisting half with medical equipment and half with sugar and we were led by General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to just focus specifically on one or two incidents on your way into Srebrenica. Now, in "War Hospital," and just for the record it's page 124, paragraph 3, it describes how the Serbs describe that the Muslims blew up the yellow bridge, but that when you heard that you thought it was the Serbs who did it to prevent the convoy from reaching Srebrenica. My question is: Is that a true reflection of what your thoughts were at the time?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. In my view, that is the truth. Why do I believe that? Because when Morillon decided that we would go to Srebrenica, for reasons I'm unaware of we were permitted and authorised to go south along the Drina on the Serbian bank, that is to pass through Mali Zvornik, to Ljubovija, along the frontier but on the Serb side of the Drina. When -- the sole entry into Bosnia was across the bridge going from Mali Zvornik to Zvornik into Bosnia. So I don't know why we took this route. We were halfway between Mali Zvornik and Ljubovija when we were stopped by a Serb police patrol or Yugoslav police patrol. And again, for reasons that Morillon himself did not understand himself, we were held there for an hour. He threatened. He said that was unacceptable. I'm going to call Milosevic. He took up his satellite telephone, which wasn't working. He went to the post office, and I don't know what was said but simply the car of the Serb police said -- went away and said we could pass. And later reaching -- I don't know exactly at what point in time this was, whether it was close to Ljubovija or Bratunac, when we were told, Unfortunately you can't go to Srebrenica because the Muslims - that was the Serbs who were saying this - had blown up the bridge. Clearly we all said it must have been the Serbs who wanted to slow us down, to prevent us reaching Srebrenica. And this was a military issue. Morillon discussed it with his people, the Canadian team that were with him, and eventually we found out that it was possible to use a route going through an old silver mine which gave its name to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry to stop you, but I want to focus again on some specifics. Again, I don't think it's in dispute that on that road or that route which you took past the old silver mine there was an incident involving a mine. Is that correct? Just yes or no and then I'll move on to another passage.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, there was a mine that went off.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, In "War Hospital" -- and I wonder if you have a copy of "War Hospital" with you or otherwise we can provide you with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, if the witness copy provided it's D199.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And are you able to read English?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's page 127, and it's seven or eight lines from the bottom. And I'll just read: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "The Bosnians are shocked that the convoy has come this way. Nobody warned them. They mined the route themselves. In fact they say a second mine is lying not far from the one that detonated. They deny knowing of any problem on the main Bratunac-Srebrenica road. They are sure the Serbs have set them up to be blamed for a catastrophe." Now, do you recall that exchange with Bosnian fighters?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, no. It was Bosnian fighters, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. As soon as this mine detonated and because the road was covered in snow, we had to leave our vehicle on this mountain road. It was very steep and it was not possible to pass. We had to continue on foot through the snow to reach the top of the mountain, where we hoped that General Morillon would be waiting for us in his armoured car and armoured vehicles of the Canadian team. Is that clear, what I have just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And if you can tell us --

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: While we were walking, after the mine went off, suddenly I saw, which I realised, were Bosniak fighters emerging from the woods next to me. We were following the road, and I saw two or three persons appearing with rifles. For a few minutes I was afraid, but they were not menacing. Apparently they heard the mine going off and they came to see what had happened. And knowing only a few words of Bosnian I said that we were internationals, that we were with the UN to reassure them. They appeared not to understand anything, and they told me that there might be another mine, which disturbed me. And they seemed to be moving without fear and they appeared to have the greatest interest in asking for a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just dealing with these fighters you encountered. Were they in uniforms or parts of uniforms? What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: They seemed to be part of the Maquis. They had old guns. They had Kalashnikov-type weapons. I don't have a great understanding of weaponry, but they seemed to be like Kalashnikovs with handles in wood. They had big jackets and hats, but not any identifiable uniforms. No rank, no insignia of the Bosnian army. We simply recognised that they were fighters because they were armed and they were wearing either a camouflage jacket or a military trousers or military boots or sometimes just a vest. And they wore just anything that they could find, but this was heterogeneous. It was not a complete uniform. We simply recognised them as fighters because they had a rifle. And I must say also their face, one could recognise a fighter by the expression he wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just -- the first sentence of your answer I don't think was adequately interpreted. I recall you say something like "Non, il y avait l'air d'etre parti de les partisans" or something of that nature. Can you repeat what you first said when I asked you what they were wearing. You said "they seemed to be" -- "they had the appearance of being part of," and that hasn't been interpreted.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: I said they had the appearance of belonging to the Maquis, the people who fight in nature, in the woods, without any political affiliation who are fighting a battle under rather savage circumstances. It is the French word, the Maquis, like the partisans.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or guerrilla fighters?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Guerrilla fighters, yes. No, people fighting in the woods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally in the transcript there was the word "makya," which attracted my attention of course but then it disappeared. So we now know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We're all clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did these people have walkie-talkies or any sort of communication devices?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: No. I wondered myself because I was rather afraid because of the explosion, and I realised that contrary to what Morillon was saying we were not being expected by the other side because we were in a most dangerous situation crossing a front line without knowing on the other side waiting for us and seeing us as a neutral force or at least being ready to accept us. So I was afraid that we might be ambushed or something. So I tried to ask them whether they could announce our arrival. I mentioned the word "Morillon" et cetera, but I saw that it was quite impossible to communicate with them except by gestures because they just said "yes, yes, okay, okay." And they had no telecommunication instrument with them. I didn't see anyone being sent to a radio position or something like that. So if we were moving more quickly than they, they didn't seem to be concerned about informing their hierarchy. So we were risking arriving there without being expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On this second visit to Srebrenica in March, how long did you stay? And when you tell us that, could you also give us a brief overview of what happened on the days that you were there.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: I stayed two nights there, one evening, one night, one day, another night, and then half a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, how did the situation seem in Srebrenica when you arrived on the 11th of March, 1993? If you could just in a few phrases explain to us the situation as you saw it.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: We arrived at night in a small town which was in a complete blackout. We arrived with the help of the lights of the Jeep and the armoured car, not the truck which was left behind but the UNHCR vehicle. And there was a crowd of people who were in a mixture of blood and -- sorry, mud and snow on the main road. There were hundreds, maybe thousands, of people who appeared to be petrified, freezing, frightened, disturbed. There wasn't a word coming from them. They didn't say "welcome" or "who are you" or "what are you doing here" why have you come." Nothing at all. There was a silence, a silence of perplexity and anxiety and nothing more. It is well-known that hospitality is sacred. People give a signal of welcome at least, and the situation was clearly dramatic beyond all expectation. And this was confirmed later on. This was my first impression. Do you wish me to continue about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask you two short questions and then -- and then you could continue. You said that there was no welcome given. Did that strike you as normal or as abnormal?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Absolutely abnormal because in December we were welcomed by people throwing flowers at us saying, "thank you for coming," "thank you for being here." And they wanted to demonstrate their encouragement for our assistance. And for them we were hope, whereas on this occasion I think the hope that the arrival of internationals could represent, in view of the situation of which they were, was no longer there -- it no longer made them move or motivated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you in terms of the people you saw, were these people who were already there in Srebrenica or were the people arriving from outside? What was that situation?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: I described the first impression I had when we left our vehicles. Quickly after that we went to greet the authorities of the town in the PTT building. My colleagues, my doctors, and the lady accompanying us, we left the meeting to try and see what the actual situation was in the hospital itself and among the population. So we left this meeting. We went to look around, and going along the main road from the post office towards the school and the hotel and the centre of the town, we noted that the situation was disastrous because the town had already been destroyed, but we saw that in December. But there were clearly people and families coming on foot, dragging crying children, old people in wheelchairs with inappropriate shoes, people trembling with cold, people who were fleeing Konjevic Polje and Cerska, which had been taken by the Serbs during the 48 hours before this. So it was terrible. I saw a man who was dragging two children with him who were crying, who had probably been walking for days. And seeing that they were in the main road of Srebrenica, they fell into the snow and fell asleep or simply to regain some strength. They were totally exhausted. One couldn't see very well because there was a total blackout. We could only use batteries. There wasn't a candle. There wasn't anything. There was absolutely no light. But the people were burning plastic bags with bottles and which apparently came from a factory in Potocari. They were making the ground burn these plastic bags [as interpreted], which provided very little light and very little warmth. And it was with the help of this light that we saw this flow of people coming into town and a vision of despair that was absolutely dramatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry to stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have an exhibit with some photographs which we're going to hand up. In the meantime there might be one interpretation issue, it may be a small thing, but the translation says you saw old people in wheelchairs. Is that what you said, wheelchairs?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, wheelbarrows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wheelbarrows, wheelbarrows.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll just explain this next exhibit. This next exhibit is photographs from Paris Match, April 1993, and I'll ask the witness to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know -- firstly, when you see the photographs can you tell us if you know who took them.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. This is a magazine that I obtained at the time, and the photos were taken by a young German photographer who was living in Srebrenica for several months, according to what I understood. He was caught up by the war, and these photographs that he took at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. Could you give us his name, please, if you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. recall it.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Philipp von Recklinghausen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think it's von Recklinghausen, actually, just for the record. Now, I'll just go through these photographs briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The first photograph, obviously General Morillon on the APC, I won't dwell on that. The second photo we see some coffins and people on the street. I would like to ask you about -- we see a young man there with a gun, a young man with a gun there. Did you see war scenes like this and people like that when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. This is a typical scene, the kind of scenes we could see the next day during the day. The photo may have taken [as interpreted] on that day precisely. Indeed this young man is very young. He has some kind of a Kalashnikov gun, a rifle. And he was part of their few armed people you could see in the town. But there were not many of them; they were rather rare. And they were supposed to maintain order, but it was just an idea. Can I tell you a story about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: The next day on the 12th of March, we were in the car and there was quite a commotion because Morillon had stated that he would leave the town and the population wanted him to stay, discuss -- negotiated with him, talked with him. And there was so many people that there were two or three people with weapons, I suppose, that were sent or came spontaneously to maintain some kind of order. I was sitting in the car, in our car that we had recovered from the place where we had left the night before, and I was some 2 or 3 metres from one of these boys. I mean, they were really young who were supposed to police a little. And one was -- there was somebody who was obviously mad, who was singing and saying nonsense. He came close, and it was something that made me startle because he came from behind, close to this boy with a weapon and he triggered the weapon. And since the weapon was directed at me, I could have received a shot in the leg or higher up. I mean, it's never very nice to have a weapon aimed at you, and this man came to trigger the weapon. I startled and this "mad" winked at me because that was a good joke. Everybody knew that the guns, the rifles, the Kalashnikovs were empty. These people who were supposed to police the situation did not have any ammunition; they were not really armed or it may be that the ammunition was somewhere else. But it was a kind of very illusory authority, just a formal thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. When you saw that person you mentioned who was supposed to be doing possibly some policing or a young man like the one in this photograph, were you able to say whether they were soldiers, fighters, civilians, policemen? Did you form an idea of who or what they were?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: No, not at all. There were no policemen; they didn't exist. The Bosnian police in Bosnia in times of Yugoslavia had some kind of grey uniforms, kind -- they looked like postmen. And you could no longer find a trace, a shadow of any such policemen anywhere. There may be a few left in Sarajevo. But there where we were, they didn't exist any longer. There were no longer police forces on the Serbian side. They were either the army or a new kind of local police, things like that. And in Srebrenica, it was total chaos. There was not a trace of a police uniform from before, from former times. There were at most some people, like this young man, who were supposed to maintain law and order, but it was totally improvised and it was totally insufficient, as was shown on several occasions later on when food was distributed, when -- at the time of the evacuation. But it was such chaos that maintaining law and order was an illusion. As to fighters, no. I mean I saw very few of them. I saw those who escorted us for an episode I didn't narrate. But once after the mine detonated we saw a truly fighting unit that took us to the centre of the town, and these were the only fighters I ever saw in Srebrenica. They were not around in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just stop you there. You've mentioned a truly fighting unit; what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Again, they had the same aspect or look. They looked like maquis resistance workers -- or fighters, sorry. They spent time in woods, bearded not shaven. They looked a little wild. I suppose the hygiene conditions were not such as to allow them -- well, I don't think that they had any logistical support. I think that they were roughing it because indeed, you know, their beards were unkept and they had totally mismatched pieces of uniforms. Two or three had some kind of white overalls, I remember. And I wondered -- I thought that they must have been overalls for snow fighting, fighting in the snow, as is the case in some armies. And I thought to myself that they must have recovered it from former stocks from the Yugoslav army. And later on I learned that they may have been overalls made from parachute canvas. And I saw two or three people wearing these very light white overalls. They were people with sort of camouflage or khaki vests or hats, but never an insignia, a rank, an indication of rank. Never anything. Sometimes they had insignia on a civilian piece of clothing. It was totally mismatched. It was impossible to know who the commander was, as far as the uniforms were concerned. And obviously people were very ill-equipped. And it was cold. I mean, there was snow and they had no gloves. Sometimes they had light clothing and they were really dirty because they had not had appear opportunity to change clothing. So it was far from being, like, a standard army with uniforms and logistical support.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask for a number to be given to this, and it's D708.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Jones, are you exhibiting the photos or also the text?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I think I should probably just exhibit the photographs since those have been commented upon. The text is there --
