utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The text is there but in other words we are not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not relying on the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So this will be D708?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you see Dr. Mujkanovic again on that visit? I think you've told us you had, but if you can describe when and how.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, I did, as early on the first evening, on the 11th of March in the night. That's the first thing we did. We asked the people there whether we could see a doctor. I gave the names of doctors I knew, Dr. Pilav, Dr. Mujkanovic, and we were told that Nedret was a bit further up, at the former Domavija Hotel. So whilst we were walking towards the hotel, we realised how dramatic the situation was in the town. Let me add a few words to answer your previous question. You must realise that this town and its population was multiplied by the number of people coming from the surrounding areas, fleeing the fighting, so displaced people, as they're called, or refugees. But there weren't any more -- I mean, only a small fraction of the original inhabitants -- it was a place where thousands of families fleeing the surrounding areas would come and they arrived in a town. There was nothing. They may never have seen this town before. And they would find no place to sleep, no shelter, no food. So there would only add up to a heap of people already in dire need. They would create this concentration of population; it could be called a town, but something that no longer had the structure of a town. Do you understand? So let me come back, if you don't mind, to this. We realised as we were walking towards the Domavija Hotel, we realised there were an amazing number of people who had sought refuge in the town. They looked anywhere for a place. They would stay in the streets. I found Dr. Mujkanovic at the Domavija Hotel. And I think we greeted each other warmly and he briefly explained what kind of a dramatic situation prevailed since December. And he was very thankful for our help; he was very happy to see us again. It was getting late. He was obviously exhausted, and he gave us a place to sleep. It was a room. There was a window but no window pane. So we had a few blankets, sort of ugly blankets, and we slept in the way locals did because there was no other condition than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If I could refer you again to "War Hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in fact it might be best if the witness keeps a copy with him, next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's -- if I direct you to page 208, if you get there -- actually that's good. You've got the photographs, and if you just turn one, two, three pages. I think you need to turn another page or two until you see a picture of Dr. Mujkanovic. And again, one more page. Now, on the left-hand side, do you see the picture on the top of Dr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have it placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, it's being placed on the ELMO so the public can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Actually, my apologies, Your Honours. I realise on the exhibit list I probably didn't list D199. That was an oversight.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm just going to direct your attention to the photograph below where there are pictures of scraps of paper and it's written: "Because of a severe paper shortage, doctors wrote prescriptions on old medical Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. records and other scraps of paper that could be found around the hospital." I just want to ask you if that's something you're aware of.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's hard to imagine how all resources were lacking in a city, a town, that had been besieged for so long. So there's a shortage in terms of heating, running water, food, down to the small things that prevent normal life, no lighting, no hygiene, just the small items of hygiene that you need just to make it possible for you to function, to operate, to communicate, to play. Children did not have balls to play with -- balloons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It didn't exist anymore, they weren't around. So indeed, at the hospital there was no paper. But that was the same in the whole town. There was no school anymore. I don't think that there were any more ballpoints around or pencils, things of that kind. So they had just adapted to the situation. They started using old patient records from the before the war that would no longer be necessary just to write out prescriptions for the pharmacy and that would deliver their medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, it's -- again, it's not in dispute that historic events occurred when General Morillon declared Srebrenica under the protection of the United Nations. I just want to ask you: Were you surprised then that happened? Did you have any thoughts or reflections when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Straight away I was aware that this was quite a historic moment, a turn in history, because I was understanding how the situation developed for a year and a half and I understood that Morillon had just taken a one-sided decision. He was certainly not supported by his hierarchy. And this was a major event because we knew that Mladic's troops were around, ready to take over the town. And then half -- a split second later I was a little afraid because I thought that the anger of the Serbian army was going to be terrible and that they could take the town even if Morillon was there. And they could do this massacre that they were about to perform whilst we were there, either by executing us or by just -- just sending us back home. So I was afraid, and I said so. I said, Now -- now there is a real problem. And I said to my colleague -- but I was sort of smiling or laughing because I was really happy that Morillon said what he said. But I understood it was then a situation we were under Serbian fire and there would be no more -- any leniency. Yes, I thought it was a bet, a gamble, a dangerous one. And I was hoping for -- wholeheartedly that Morillon would win it, this gamble. And that had been so not just that day, but for months. But then I understood that it was really quite a historic moment and it was a risky thing, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move forward a bit to an exhibit -- or a new document which will be handed around. And it's -- for the record, it's a fax which was sent to -- under the heading (redacted) from (redacted) and it's dated 17th April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: While that's being handed around, did you provide that document to me when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And could you tell us who (redacted) is?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: (redacted) was this young lady who was my assistant in Belgrade, and she was with us, too, on the 11 or 12th of March, 1993, in Srebrenica. She's not a doctor, but she speaks very good Russian and she was learning Serbo-Croat. And we thought that if we were going with a translator, a Serbian translator or a Bosnian translator or Croatian translator, problems might ensue at the checkpoint. Therefore, she offered quite bravely or courageously to come with us. Normally we only took doctors with us, but she wanted to work as a translator so it was quite brave of her.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now this, correct me if I'm wrong, contains a report on Srebrenica. The first page refers to Milici, and that doesn't concern us. The second page, "mission Srebrenica, 28/3 - 4/4." And can you confirm the year that that would refer to.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. These are the first weeks during the Srebrenica mission after General Morillon had more or less succeeded in holding back the Serbian attack and until the zone was declared as a safe area, diplomatically speaking. So towards the end of March, three weeks or two weeks after we entered the town with Morillon. These are the first medical observations aimed at organising the aid programme that we wanted to set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So March to April 1993?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just want to take you to two parts of this report. The first, if you have 1, "situation au debut", the hospital; and then the second point "activities," and then there's a phrase there, [Interpretation ] "before the cease-fire up to the 30 wounded per day." Now, was that the information you received from your (redacted) subordinates in Srebrenica, that before the cease-fire there were up to 30 injuries a day?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: You mean me personally? What are you asking me? Did I receive this information before? Beforehand we had no information at all, not a trace, not even the barest minimum. The only information available about Srebrenica came through the government radio in Sarajevo. Apparently they had some radio contact with Srebrenica. They described a disastrous situation, but we did not regard this as objective information when it comes to public health. It was not measurable. So I had no information whatsoever before going back in person on the 11th of March, nothing at all. But as to this figure of 30 injuries per day, that seems quite reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me approach this also this way. This is addressed to (redacted). Is this a fax that you actually received in your capacity as head of (redacted) head of mission?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. (redacted) was in charge of our mission at the Brussels headquarters and this report had been established by a (redacted). She had interviewed the doctors and the engineer who had gone through Srebrenica -- well, who were in Srebrenica. So -- and she did that because I couldn't do everything and she gave me a copy and that's when I apprised myself on the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like you to turn to the second page now and this is dealing with apparently a school which is a refugee centre, and it appears that there was an enquete there, a check-up of 150 persons. I want to ask you about the entry that says "Scabies, pediculis, 80 to 90 pct." Can you explain for us what that entry means?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: No. There were more people in this corps. Mention is made of 7 to 800 people; that's a lot. I mean, it was totally overcrowded, that's on the previous page. And they carried out an inquiry of having a sampling of some 150 people to have some reasonable idea of the problems faced by most of the people in the school. So what I can read here is simply that 15 per cent - "pct," that's per cent - 15 per cent of the people suffered from diarrhea, 10 per cent from respiratory problems, airways problems, and 90 per cent had scabies. And lice, pediculis in French [as interpreted]. Another relevant thing is that over 50 per cent of the people suffered from anemia, a lack of iron in the blood or red cells, and that could be clinically observed. So they had the smooth tongue, for instance, which shows a major weakening of the body. Over half of the people were clinically anaemic, which goes to show that there is a major deprivation and prolonged deprivation of food and vitamins.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On the basis of what you saw in this report, would it be fair to say that there were a lot of people in Srebrenica in March/April 1993 who looked in very poor condition?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: No. It's wrong to say so. The situation was of extreme, out-of-the ordinary deprivation. It's hard to perceive such a situation except in war situation that had probably not been seen probably since the Second World War. It's not just a situation of poverty or lacking some things, both from the point of view of health, public health, or in everyday life, accommodation, hygiene, privacy, private space, any possibility of having some kind of formal social structure or getting organised. These people were under constant torture. What I mean is they were both in the situation where their vital, their primary needs were not met, I mean food, health, just surviving, and at the same time they were under shelling, they were under constant fear, they could fear that they would be attacked, that they were threatened. So they were in a sort of self-perpetuating chaos because there were constant new arrivals of refugees. It was impossible to build anything because all the -- I mean, there were an increasing -- decrease of resources. You couldn't go hunting. A little bit of agricultural activity that there was was gone. Gone. So everything was wearing out; it was disappearing. It is a situation of extreme torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just want to ask specifically about scabies. As a doctor, can you just describe to us what are the symptoms of scabies and what's the appearance of someone who has scabies?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, well the main symptom of scabies is that it's itch -- itching. You can't help itching because the parasite is under the skin. It is an acarian that gets under the skin creating small tunnels, very simple, but it provokes terrible itching. And you can see that someone has scabies because people really itch and scratch themselves until they bleed. It's a very difficult disease when it becomes invading. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- right.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Very debilitating.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Final on this document where it's referring to the amount of nourriture. It says "distribution of 100 grams of bread and a glass of milk a day." Can you explain what in layman's terms what 100 grams of food amounts to, what an example would be?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Well, 100 grams of bread, well -- is half a sandwich. So a little bun like this, bread roll, small one. Well, when you have a loaf, a big family loaf, that's about 1 kilo. So 100 grams would be a tenth of that. It's a very small portion of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it a sufficient amount to live on over a long period?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: No, no, of course not. No, it's really not sufficient; far from it. It is obvious people did not have enough food to live in Srebrenica. It's way below the necessary amount to survive in proper conditions without damaging your health.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask for the exhibit number for this document, please. I think it's D709.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document consisting of one, two, three, four, five, six pages originating from (redacted) is being tendered -- everything is -- is being marked as exhibit number -- Defence Exhibit Number D709. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have another document now which we'll hand up which is an article from the Lancet, which is a medical journal, volume 341, 8th of May, 1993, pages 1193 to 1196.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, I'll just ask, did you provide this document to me when you arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... of this article in preparing the article?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. I was interviewed at some length by the authors of this document, specifically about what happened in Srebrenica, because I think they themselves never went there. And I was asked for -- kindly to make a contribution for this document. And then they sent it to me afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I only have one question on this document which is: On the second page, the right-hand column, the bottom of the top photograph, you see there it says: "The convoy that reached Srebrenica on March 19 after the commander of UN Protection Forces established temporary headquarters in the town contained food that was sufficient for less than five days' energy needs for the 60.000 inhabitants." And I would simply ask you whether that figure sounds approximately correct or not.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. The quantity of food quite, because it was carefully measures by the UNHCR. The figure of 60.000 inhabitants is an estimate, obviously. One could never have this number checked because the whole area of Srebrenica was spread out beyond the centre of the town, and it was clearly very difficult to find out how many people were actually living there. Maybe 50.000 would be closer than 60.000, which would mean that they had food for six days rather than five.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll just ask for an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document extracted from the Lancet of May 8th, 1993, volume 341, from page 1193 to page 1196 is being tendered and received and marked as Defence Exhibit D710.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you, Dr. Dachy, to take up "War Hospital" again and to turn to page 101. And I'll read the paragraph into the record since not everyone has copies. And it's a passage which describes Nedret, Dr. Mujkanovic, travelling to the field to watch actions. And it's the quote at the very bottom of 101 going over to 102. "It is the rumbling of their empty stomachs which sets these hapci," that's the word for civilians who were going into action as hapci, "on the heels of the soldiers. They come from hunger and need and anger, many of them displaced from their own homes. Nedret sees them raging out of control disobeying directives not to destroy things." And it says, "The Serb civilians lie dead in their wake," i.e. the wake of the hapci. The question I want to ask you is did you make any observation or form any opinion, clinical or otherwise, then or subsequently, regarding the behaviour of very hungry people subject to conditions such as you saw in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with observations first, Mr. Jones, and then come to the second point later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please specify the first part of your question for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Did you make any observations concerning the behaviour of very hungry people subject to conditions such as you saw in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. It was something quite disturbing because I had experience with Kurdish refugees in Iraq who were in a dramatic situation, and I also saw a cholera epidemic in Africa among displaced persons. So I began to have a quite considerable experience as to the way in which people live when they find themselves in situations fighting for survival. When their life is at risk and when they take radical decisions such as to flee, to dislocate their families, et cetera. Srebrenica was especially impressive because there was a concentration of many elements. First of all, quite clearly, everyone there was traumatised. They were in a trauma. This was a traumatising situation every day, but a multi-dimensional situation because at the same time they feared shells that were coming regularly. Then again there was hunger, then simple things like children not having shoes of the necessary size, children crying because their shoes were too small. And these people found themselves in this dramatic situation, fearing for their very survival, and at the same time being unable to provide the essentials for themselves and their families. So this applied to big things as to small. And systematically the people were condemned to powerlessness. They were confined to this area, subject to bombardment, then exposed to constant hunger, and this went on for months and months. There was the period of autumn, winter, and spring, and this was an impossible situation. And the majority of people became desperate at the same time and in a slight delirium even. They were disillusioned, they had to struggle with these very small things and even these small things were a great problem because the situation was totally degrading. Then people attach themselves to the past, trying to reconstruct their lives, but in Srebrenica this was impossible because the threat of death was there on a daily basis and the people really had nothing to hope for, nothing to attach themselves to on a daily basis to hold on to. So there was a process of psychological degradation which, in my opinion - and this is a conviction on my part - that this was absolutely deliberate on the part of the Serbs. Ethnic cleansing and everything else was implemented by a deliberate intention to dehumanise the enemy. The political theory was: The Muslims don't exist, they are Serbs and Croats that have converted to Islam. And during the war they were treated like animals, executed en masse, deported, cleansed. And in this war of a siege of the town, like in all such wars, there was a psychological siege, to subject the enemy to psychological desperation and degradation and to discourage them. And this worked. The Serbs could easily bomb the centre of town when they wanted. They could have done that in the case of the football pitch, but they didn't do it. They could have done it. They were observed through binoculars; they knew what was happening in town. And this was a strategy; that is, to psychologically degrade the population. And this went beyond simply being hungry or needing something. This was this prolonged inability to meet essential needs of one's own and one's family, and this continued ceaselessly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to move on to a new area now. After you left Srebrenica in March 1993 I think you've told us and it's clear from the facts, you continued to monitor the situation. I want to deal with a very specific issue concerning a water-treatment plant in Srebrenica, and I'd be grateful if you can tell us about that plant and any events surrounding it.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: With respect to the activities of the (redacted) for displaced and refugee populations, we developed a certain ability to intervene, to take care of medical needs, food, shelter, sheltering the people when they have nowhere to go, and the provision of drinking water. These are four areas in which we had competent persons and standard material that we used. And we were equipped to use them, and we had action plans for this. And clearly from our very arrival in Srebrenica, we asked ourselves the question of drinking water, which was lacking. There was no drinking water. And the person who entered Srebrenica immediately after me was an engineer specialising in water, (redacted), and his mission was to observe the population's needs with respect to water. Because in Srebrenica, as in other parts of the world, the shortage of drinking water can be the source of the gravest epidemics and it's better to prevent and to treat and it's much better to provide drinking water than to treat epidemics.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I can stop you there because I'd like to take this issue very Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. quickly before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like to pass up the next exhibit which deals with this and we have copies for everyone. It's a telex -- appears or purposes to be a telex from (redacted) Srebrenica to (redacted) Brussels, 16th September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I continue with Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to use this document and take it step by step. I'm just going to read, it's the second page under 3, "water and sanitation" -- I'm sorry, before that: Did you provide this document to me when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, page 2, 3, "water and sanitation." It says: "(redacted) runs also a water and sanitation programme in Srebrenica. The city is without water since May and is surviving on 2 to 3 litres of drinking water per person per day. The water treatment plant Zeleni Jadar was captured by the Bosnian Serbs in April and blown up by them in June when UN and (redacted) mission asked permission to start it up again." And if you could just confirm with a yes or no whether you recall that information.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I recall it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in fact, I'll ask now for an exhibit number for this document. I'm going to use it again later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will become Defence Exhibit D711, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this is also dealt with on pages 205 to 207 of "War Hospital," in particular 206, and I think they're also -- that would help to clarify the name of the person of the (redacted) engineer. On page 206, third paragraph it says: "If there is no access to Zeleni Jadar, this city will fall soon without water," (redacted) telexes Eric in Belgrade. “I have the impression that nobody outside of Srebrenica takes this seriously. The whole world needs to realise that this town will be strangled in several days if they do nothing." First of all, can you confirm (redacted) last name?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we have another exhibit which is related to this and it's two documents which need to be read together. The first is from the command of the Drina Corps, dated 31 May 1993. The ERN is 04294404. And I'll read -- it's the -- the main paragraph. And it states: "Lieutenant-Colonel Urosevic received a verbal order from the commander, Colonel Milenko Jovanovic, to demolish the water tower and tank in the area of Zeleni Jadar, water supply system for Srebrenica. Since this has not been done so far, this task is to be executed immediately by June 1, 1993, at the latest, and it is to be presented to the public as if the Muslim forces did it." "And it is to be presented to the public as if the Muslim forces did it." Now, my question is this: You told us about your suspicions about the yellow bridge being destroyed by Serbs and then claiming that the Muslims did it. Based on your knowledge of the war in Yugoslavia and use of propaganda, would something like this surprise you, this document?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I think so that that is how things happened, because the way in which (redacted)described it to me is quite in accordance with this. Do you wish me to explain? I realised this at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In a moment. I just want to deal quickly with the second document since they're together, and that's Drina Corps command dated 21 June 1993, ERN 04294708, and it refers to: "Submit the data on the Muslim DTG that demolished the water supply system in Zeleni Jadar. Since we need to inform highest UNPROFOR bodies about the barbaric act of the Muslim DTG when they demolished the water supply system in Zeleni Jadar, and on this occasion directly confronted our forces. Inform me of the following: According to your estimation how many terrorists took part in this demolition action. Briefly describe the sequence of events and in the direct clash with our forces whether you've killed, wounded heavily or lightly, or captured any terrorists."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'll ask for an exhibit number before we proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document consists of two documents basically. I know that they are related, connected, one with the other. Do you want to tender them together?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why I'd prefer that, yes, so they'll always before together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you. So this document consists of basically two documents bearing the following ERN numbers, in B/C/S, 04294404 and 04294708, are being tendered together and marked as Defence Exhibits D712.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And yes, if there is anything from what (redacted) told you which reflects on the exhibit we just saw, then please do go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: I'd simply tell you of the way in which (redacted) told me at the time, because we knew immediately that the question of drinking water was essential for the survival of the population and it was of vital urgency. 9 And I kept in touch with (redacted) on a daily basis about it, and he started by telling me that at Zeleni Jadar there was a water treatment plant which was quite functional. And he went there with the Canadian blue helmets and looking at it and examining it, he was able to see that it could be maintained and -- as it was absolutely functional. And the only thing that prevented maintenance was that it was under Serb fire for a long period of time. So he said to himself, I'm going to make it operational. And when he returned, he asked through UNPROFOR that access to that area be secured and guaranteed by the Serbs. And he told me that the Serb reply was that the water treatment plant had been blown up, and clearly it was not by the inhabitants or the defence of Srebrenica that had access to that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to go back to exhibit -- I think it's D711 now, which is the telex which we saw. And it's -- at the very top of page 3 where it refers to: "The overcrowding in Srebrenica is beyond any standard. 90 per cent of all houses and buildings are damaged by the war." And then further down we see it's written that: "Bricks were recuperated from totally destroyed houses." Sorry, I'm just finding that again now. Yes, it's in the third paragraph. "Bricks were recuperated from totally destroyed houses." Now, did you receive information from the field to the effect that refugees were going and getting building materials like bricks from destroyed houses in this area?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: From the area, yes. We ourselves organised a programme intending to repair houses that could be repaired with plastic sheeting mostly, but also bringing tools which would allow pulling out nails and repairing houses, and this was done by -- in 1993 at the beginning by (redacted) who in this way managed to rehabilitate a part of the town. And he was called (redacted) because he had the ability of an architect. He collected material, and this was something which was absolutely necessary, to collect material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection, Your Honours. I'm trying to understand this part of the witness better. Mr. Jones can clarify, I'm sure, but is the witness speaking about programmes that were put into effect following his visit in March 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understand it -- MR. DI FAZIO: But I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understand it for the time being, and correct me if I'm wrong, this takes us to September 1993, this telex. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The previous two documents about the destruction of the water-treatment plant we're talking about June of 19 -- May is the date of the first document for the 1st of June for the destruction of the water plant. MR. DI FAZIO: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it seems that happened around the 21st of June. MR. DI FAZIO: That's why I think that, but I just wanted to be absolutely certain about the time period --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can clarify with the witness the time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know if it's useful for me to clarify the point, maybe it's an obvious one, but we've seen photographs from 1995 of houses. I'm exploring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not stopping you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Dachy, can you clarify for us when this activity carried out by (redacted) occurred?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: A few weeks between April and August 1993, for a few weeks. I no longer remember exactly the dates when he was there but he was part of the first programme that we set up in Srebrenica. So it was during the summer. I would say shortly after April -- maybe May. Is that sufficient as an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm coming to just one or two final areas --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So this might be an appropriate moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. That means we will reconvene at 10 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I should just mention that I'll probably be finished within 10 or 15 minutes something that Mr. Di Fazio --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's up to you, Mr. Di Fazio, whether you want to start today or -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'll finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You'll finish today? MR. DI FAZIO: It's my plan to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Dr. Dachy, I just have three last areas to cover with you. Firstly, I was asking you about propaganda by the Serbs in relation to property destruction. I want to ask you: From your base in Belgrade, did you come across any forms of propaganda by the Serb authorities, either relating to the war in Croatia or in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, that's the only thing I came across actually. Any piece of information, any information, whether it be sports, any news or facts, was constantly interpreted through this prism of the hostility, the antagonism between Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks. It was re-interpreted through a new reading of history, a new understanding of history where Serbs were always the victims of their wish to be free.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were the images shown on the news, for example, in that relation?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, all the time. For instance, the European Union was systematically presented as being the embodiment, the finalisation of the Nazi dream which is the European unification dominated by Germany. That was already the picture reported of the European Union, the image. But as to daily propaganda, war-related propaganda, as soon as I arrived in October of 1991 I noticed, for instance, on prime time, the news -- 7.00 news on RTB, the Radio and Television Belgrade, the official public television channel in Serbia, pictures were shown. Atrocious pictures were shown of mutilated bodies, of children with their eyes gouged out, with cut ears, throats slit. It was abominable and it was presented at a time when children watched TV, and from what I was told that was also shown in the afternoon or noon news. And though I was skeptical, it was obvious -- I thought some of the wounds must have been caused post mortem because they didn't look like injuries to a living body or just a body that has just died. The -- the flesh did not react, so it was quite shocking and I remember how shocking it was even for me, emotionally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm leaving that area and I'm going back to D711 just for the conclusions in that document and just again -- as a reminder for the record it's the document of 16 September, 1993. When did you actually -- how long did you stay in Bosnia for?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Altogether in Yugoslavia, I stayed two years and a half during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that takes us, I imagine, to -- perhaps you can help us with that. You arrived in October 1991, so early 1994 you left. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, the conclusion -- I just want to read two sentences from that and then pose a question to you. It says: "The population of Srebrenica is completely isolated from the outside world and is forced into self-sufficiency. However, it is impossible to provide the structure for self-sufficiency in the short term or even in the long term as long as the Bosnian Serbs are ruling the area. There are no local resources and there is no energy source. There are no institutions and there are no people and material to start up these institutions." It then gives the example of the hospital, which you have spoken about at length. And then further down it says: "The hospital is only one example of the numerous other social and legal institutions which need to be created. They all face the same problems. There are no qualified persons available to run these institutions and they will not come from Sarajevo or Tuzla. The idea of a self-sufficient enclave surrounded by a hostile population is a complete illusion. The UN declared Srebrenica as a safe haven, but in fact sold it to the Bosnian Serbs who are turning it slowly into a legal extermination camp." I want to ask you firstly do you know who in fact wrote this -- this telex, who the author is?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The team working in Srebrenica did it on the basis of sort of a conclusion or analysis of the fist months they worked there. (redacted) is one of the authors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you mention names because this always worries me. Are these necessary for you, Mr. Jones, because sometimes these people will be on the field somewhere --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- else in the world and their names and identities may need to be protected. I don't know whether Dr. Dachy has been in contact with (redacted) before coming here and whether there's any concern on behalf or on the part of (redacted) to have names protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your concerns, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If they are important for you, go ahead. If Mr. Dachy thinks he can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think for one Mr. Dachy has been in contact with (redacted) and he can -- if required, he can explain that. It's sufficient our purposes to have the name of (redacted) just for one. And he's on our witness list and I have been in contact with him and he's no longer with the organisation as far as I understand. But that's sufficient for our purposes and I appreciate Your Honour intervening at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, my question is: There the hospital is spoken of as an example of social and legal institutions which face the same problems in Srebrenica. Is that something you agree or disagree with, that the hospital is, if you like, a paradigm for the other social and political institutions in Srebrenica at that time? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please, unless the witness has a basis for being able to comment on the situation that faced the -- in particular I'm concerned about of course is the political institutions that existed in Srebrenica. We all know what I'm talking about. Unless the witness can demonstrate a basis for commenting on that, then I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but the report or this telex itself seems to deal with that. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would take it -- if they are reporting on such a matter and on the need to sort of rebuild from scratch all these institutions, legal and social, to the -- to (redacted) in Paris -- MR. DI FAZIO: I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would -- and Brussels, I would imagine they know what they are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you like, I'm happy to withdraw the question and let the document speak for itself. That's probably easiest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm satisfied with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ultimately that's what the document says. I would expect whoever drafted this document to have drafted it in a responsible manner and not -- MR. DI FAZIO: I -- that might be so, Your Honour, I'm not talking about that. The question was actually asking this witness to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: And that's what I was concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, it's no longer the case, so please proceed, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I will ask for your comment on one final passage if you are able to. It's the passage which says -- it's on the second page or page 4, actually, three paragraphs down: "When UNPROFOR arrived in March, people thought it was the end of the nightmare and there was a general optimism. This optimism turns into bitterness now. Everybody realises that the tragedy is not far off." This is dated September 1993. Is it or was it your experience understanding that there were warnings of something catastrophic in Srebrenica in September 1993 and indeed from the time of your visit?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: When we came in March 1993, the disaster was really not far off at all because there was this takeover, question of the takeover of the town by the Serb troops. And that was a proven fact and that would mean death and devastation for thousands of people. When this fax was written, the situation has evolved somewhat because the zone, the area, had become a safe area which was officially protected by the United Nations. What this fax is pointing to is that the status given to this town did not make it possible to really survive, and that was a real problem. It was obvious to me. I totally agreed with the contents of this fax because it seemed obvious to me that the intervention by General Morillon and the ensuing negotiations with demilitarisation of the zone and the safe-haven status given to the town was a relative protection, but let's not forget that other places had been declared safe havens or safe areas; it didn't mean much. I had the feeling that it might have a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. positive effect in as much as it would have sort of halted a Serb attack that would have been very bloody. But I, like many other people, thought that that was not enough as a status and it was necessary to keep on working on that basis, diplomatically, from the humanitarian point of view, and possibly militarily, so that the population could have some better conditions. If it remained sort of imprisoned in this status, it could only expect worse, not as bad as the town being taken by the Serbs. But it was in no way the situation that could grant them some decent minimal living conditions, acceptable ones. Do I answer your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, perfectly. Thank you. And finally, at the beginning of your testimony today you mentioned the name "Naser Oric." Did you come to hear -- to hear about him while you were in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. As I told you, this was the name associated with resistance, a spontaneous resistance by the Bosniaks in Eastern Bosnia. I heard this name mentioned the first time in Belgrade, and it was linked to the name of Srebrenica. It was the name given to resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you form any impressions of Naser Oric during your stay or -- of what -- let me put it this way: March 1993 when you were in Srebrenica, did you form any impressions about him in a general -- in a general manner?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: In a general manner, our impression was a positive one. It was clearly somebody who was always mentioned with a lot of respect, but more than respect, with a fondness. Everybody called him Naser, so much so that even in the United Nations people ended up talking about him as Naser. And I found that really telling because most leaders or commanders have war names or prestigious names with ranks, Captain this or Colonel that. In fact, the people from Srebrenica just said "Naser." So the way they would speak about him showed that he was a very accessible person. In March 1993, it was of course difficult to confirm this impression because we didn't stay long. But I was the main person in charge responsible for the good running of missions. I was in charge of delicate negotiations with political and military institutions. My first strategy was to avoid contacts with people unless they were absolutely necessary. So I did -- I was not keen on meeting Naser Oric any more than I was keen on meeting political or military leaders because often, you know, they would present conditions for assistance. They could be sort of horse trading, and we were used to that with Serbs. So in the early months, the experience was the most crucial one and I -- being modest, I can tell you that I was in very close contact -- I was trying to monitor the work done by the team in Srebrenica proper because I was in contact with -- with a team by CapSat, and I told them that they should be very prudent, very cautious not to make promises and to avoid contacts with authorities, as much as that was possible. But to really focus on our partnership with the medical staff in the hospital. They were our natural partner. And all this was confirmed. And this positive impression that I had of Naser Oric was confirmed because I learned that he sometimes went to the hospital, that he was a very simple in the way that he was, that he was very kind, not too -- not overly demonstrative or controlling. And that made a very positive impression on me because this is -- anywhere you are in the world, this is very exceptional. Humanitarian aid is always part of the things that can be negotiated, that are at stake for any fighter, for authorities, for anybody in power, and there are exceptional situations. Such was the situation in Srebrenica. And in such situations, any abuse can happen and grow because there's no more containment or break on the institution. There's no more social or political democratic break. And I was always struck by the fact that we never had a problem with Naser Oric, called Naser by everybody, or anybody claiming to belong to his group or represent him. Later on after the war, I received very personal testimony from people I knew who conveyed a very positive image of this person. Could I maybe mention somebody?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe this would be the last matter, since during the course of these trials we actually have to present mitigation as we go along. Rather than recalling Dr. Dachy during the course of proofing, there is a matter which relates to 1995, it's a brief testimony, just a few lines. If the witness could read that, and then we can conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll just explain the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection on your part? MR. DI FAZIO: None, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you explain the context, please.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: This is what happened after 1995 and after the fall of the enclave, a dreadful escape of thousands of people through woods and hills. (redacted) gathered testimony systematically from people who had survived this death march. Personally I knew the translator who translated the interviews. There were scores of audio-cassettes where all this was recorded to know what happened. And this female translator said - I knew her personally - She said, It's unbelievable. People really love Naser Oric. He is the one who is most in their memories, and they're very thankful to him because he's the one who came to help them cross the last lines in an area called Bajkovica where people would arrive walking. And she said that in a general way, and that was confirmed because on several occasions I visited people, survivors, in Tuzla, survivors of the escape from Srebrenica. They always confirmed this very positive impression. But I want to stick to an objective document and I want to quote the transcript done in August 1995 of a young woman, Ramiza. She was 18 then and she tells how she arrived in Bajkovica. It was quite an apocalyptic journey where she saw dead and wounded. She said: "I didn't cry in spite of all this suffering, and when I saw the commander, Naser Oric, when I saw him cry, I started crying myself. I did not think that I had arrived at my destination. That's why I cried." So other people always conveyed this image of somebody who's a very decent human and from my personal experience, which is of course limited, it was never changed by facts or other convincing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, do you want to have access to this documents that the witness was reading from or is it -- isn't it necessary for you? MR. DI FAZIO: No, it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not planning to exhibit it because it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, actually -- this is what I expected from Mr. Di Fazio, the kind of answer I expected from Mr. Di Fazio, so it -- any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I can't provide that guarantee that I provided to you earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, tomorrow we are scheduled to continue with the case in the afternoon. So if the witness is not done, we'll continue with him tomorrow. He doesn't have to travel fast -- travel far, I mean, he doesn't have to travel far. And in two hours he'll be in Brussels, so he can go, sleep there, and come back tomorrow if he wants to. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Dr. Dachy, I won't be too long with you. Earlier this morning you said you attended meetings, coordination meetings, with UN bodies like the High Commissioner for Refugees and so on and that there you came to know of the name "Naser Oric." Which meetings are you referring to and am I correct that you are referring to meetings that occurred before November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. As soon as I arrived in Belgrade, I was invited to regular meetings of governmental organisations, organised by the UNHCR, which was designated as the coordinated body for all the agencies. And I think every fortnight there was a meeting. The agenda was conveyed to us. There were information meetings, which included the UNHCR, but also UNICEF, the International Red Cross or the Committee for the Red Cross, or the Federation; international handicapped organisations, (redacted), and others. And these were meetings of coordination to discuss what to do and what had been done to avoid gaps in the provision of aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Does that answer your question? So it was before November 1992. In fact, it was then that I heard mention of Srebrenica and Naser Oric. That was already in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And was that -- you heard the name, I take it, during the actual course of meetings with the bodies that you have mentioned in your previous answer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And is it the case that there was a common theme that went through these -- what you heard about Mr. Oric at these meetings and to, if I may quote your very own words, "the name given to the resistance in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Srebrenica was 'Naser Oric.'" Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. And the name Naser Oric and his role as the embodiment of the resistance came up during the course of conversations or discussions you were having with these aid organisations when you were discussing what was going on in Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, but we couldn't even talk about what was happening in Srebrenica. His name and the name of Srebrenica was mentioned in the context of something happening there which could easily motivate humanitarian intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But there's no doubt about it, to quote your own words: "'Naser Oric' was the name that was given to the resistance," at least in these initial meetings that you had in the summer of 1992? I see you nodding but we need a yes or no for the purposes of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, quite. I was waiting for the end of the translation. I confirm what you said. Yes, I heard mention of Naser Oric as being the incarnation of resistance in Eastern Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he described as a good leader, a brave and courageous commander?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: During the meetings of coordination at the UN, everyone was extremely cautious in his use of words for an enormous number of reasons, which are quite understandable, the first being that this was not a place where we were to make any judgements or political speculations. And this was of the greatest importance. So it's a little more complicated than that because it was clear that for security reasons and in order to know where we were moving, it was also important to exchange information as to where Arkan and his forces were because it could be very dangerous. There was someone who was almost killed in cold blood, but we sought to collect information about the degree of danger of actors that we might encounter in certain areas. In that sense we may have evoked, shall we say, the dangerous character of the area where Naser Oric was one of the leaders. And I must say that the Bosniak resistance in that region never represented any danger for international workers. For instance, Mr. Mendiluce who was the head of the UN, right down to the driver. We did not have any fear of the Bosniak defence, which is quite different from what could happen in Sarajevo where crossing the front line was extremely dangerous and one would never know who might fire on us. So quite clearly, Naser Oric was not someone who was spoken of as being dangerous for us humanitarians. As for making any political judgements, as from the summer of 1992 the presence of regrouping camps or concentration camps whereby ethnic cleansing was carried out, this was not something that we could make any judgement, political judgement, of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Dr. Dachy --

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: -- even negative judgement because we might be portrayed as defending ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Dr. Dachy, thank you for that but I think you've answered my question. Thank you very much. In the period of time before your trip in November of 1992 into the Srebrenica area, did (redacted) put in -- or start to make plans for an anticipated provision of aid to people in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because we are not -- I understood the witness of course, but and I think for those who can't understand French we need interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are asking me whether in December 1992 I had intentions to provide aid to the population of Srebrenica? MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have to either rephrase it a little bit to make it clear to the witness because it's actually two things that you asked of him, and one would be immediate; the other one is future. So I leave it in your hands, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the months preceding -- months preceding November of 1992, did (redacted) start to make plans for the provision of aid, I assume medical aid, to people within the Srebrenica area, the people surrounded by hostile Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. Quite clearly, yes. Our intention was and our -- it was our priority to be able to provide aid to Srebrenica. However, as I have already explained, all my attempts to ask for permission from the authorities of the Serb Republic of Bosnia came across an absolute barrier, and I was responsible for that type of strategic effort. And I thought that the Srebrenica zone was isolated and the needs in terms of medical needs were very considerable. So clearly, that was our intention but it was not possible for us to carry it into practice because we were not able to freely circulate in that area and the humanitarian principles that we referred to, even with Karadzic, did not bear fruit. Nobody could go to Srebrenica: The UN, the International Red Cross Committee, absolutely no one could enter Srebrenica with the exception of a few people who entered secretly, but in a way that did not allow for humanitarian aid to be delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move to another area, if I may. The -- just moments ago as you were finishing your examination-in-chief, Mr. Jones asked you about Mr. Oric. And you again said that this was the name associated with resistance in Eastern Bosnia, and you again reminded us that you heard his name first mentioned in Belgrade and it was the name given to resistance. In the period of time from when you arrived in Belgrade up until November of 1992, did you continually hear of the name Naser Oric being linked to the resistance in Eastern Bosnia, and in particular Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite clearly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that -- you said that -- just bear with me for a moment, please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said that: "Eventually even people in the United Nations ended up talking about him as 'Naser.'" Can you tell us a bit more about that. What United Nations people are you talking about? And are you referring to the period of time before November 1992 when you first went into Srebrenica, the people -- the United Nations people who called him Naser?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: No. I was referring to the period that followed after December 1992, that is the period, or rather after March when international workers were able to contact the population of Srebrenica. And the people I alluded to, I think I can quote their names, Roland Gentille or even Hollingworth, even the soldiers on the ground would say Naser because the people on the ground called him Naser. It simply reflected closeness, when you refer to someone in the way he is referred to by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Oric was a man who, was fair to say, known throughout the Srebrenica enclave as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes, it was known -- he was known. He was someone with a reputation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Everyone would know him. People you met in the streets in November and March of 1993, the name Naser was known to everyone, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think it's a bit much to -- MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Everyone that you met anyway?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- ask about 60.000 people in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he's qualified it now. Otherwise your objection would have made sense of this. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Everyone you met in those trips November 1992, March 1993, when you're walking around in the streets, dealing with the problems you had to deal with, carrying out our duties, speaking to people. Everyone knew who Naser Oric was, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: It is rather difficult to answer with respect to this period because I had an obstacle because of lack of knowledge of the language and I couldn't speak to the population. And the last majority of the population were peasants who had fled from the surroundings and who arrived there. And the town to us was a mystery to the extent of knowing how much people knew because people didn't have papers, radio, television for so long, that so many things may have escaped them. They lived in a world marked by fear where rumours could circulate and they existed. I'm not so sure that people knew Naser, but what impressed me was the people in the hospital, for instance, did not speak of him as a president or a commander of the region that should be referred to when there was something to be decided, but rather they referred to him with a certain familiarity, as a companion, as a friend, as someone with charm and influence. And with the doctors in the hospital from time to time Naser was mentioned. And as I kept at a distance from everything that might be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. an authority, I understood that they referred to him as someone close but not someone they feared, whose decisions and orders and feared. And this was confirmed later on when I was told that he made brief visits to the hospital out of pure interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not suggesting for one minute that Mr. Oric presented as an authoritarian figure. You said in your evidence in reply to a question from Mr. Jones concerning any impression that you formed about Mr. Oric in general, you said this -- I think it must be: "He was clearly somebody who was always mentioned with a lot of respect, but more than respect with a fondness. Everybody called him Naser, so much so that even in the United Nations people ended up talking about him as Naser." Now, I'm not asking you about the United Nations, but you did say that: "Everybody called him Naser." Now that's everybody in Srebrenica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will solve itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a colloquialism.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's I'm telling you to sit down because we are dealing with a professional man, so I don't think it needs any explanations. Yes, Dr. Dachy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to give you a precise answer. It's clear that Naser Oric was a well-known figure. I heard him referred to even in Belgrade, and clearly in Srebrenica the people that I visited, important people, doctors, nurses in the hospital, knew who Naser was. And what impressed me was that whoever spoke of him called him "Naser." Does that answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't -- Mr. Di Fazio, you're free to ask all the questions you like on this matter, but I don't think we are going to advance more than this. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't think so either, Your Honours. I'll just -- This is the only area of interest that I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no it's up to you. Because we are back to square one on this matter. After a series of three or four questions -- so it's the doctors, the nurses, the people he spoke to at Belgrade, whatever, and that's not going to change. MR. DI FAZIO: I agree. I've just about finished in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can bring the witness again tomorrow. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm hoping to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just one other small area that I want to ask you about, and again from the answer that you gave towards the end of your testimony. You said -- talking about people calling him Naser you found that -- "I found that really telling because most leaders or commanders have the rank or name with colonel this. In fact the people from Srebrenica just said Naser." In other words, you regarded him as the commander, didn't you, the commander in the area, military commander?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: That is a notion that was conveyed to me but which for me was something that had to be verified and confirmed. Because in regions such as this you hear someone mentioned as being of importance, but you never know who has the power --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That may be so --

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: -- and to what extent --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: -- that may be so but I'm asking you about your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's an objection to saying "the commanders," because the witness's answer is normally commanders and leaders have, essentially, a nom de guerre. "A commander" would be a fair question, not the commander. It doesn't follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't stop Mr. Di Fazio from putting the question the way he put it because obviously it's meant to solicit an answer from the witness as to whether there was only one real commander and whether that one real commander was indeed Naser Oric or not. This is what is being put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness can answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's why -- because I anticipated what your objection was going to be. Yes, please, Mr. Di Fazio, please go ahead. If you want to repeat your question or whatever, it's up to you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In other words, you regarded him as the commander or leader, didn't you, in the area?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: No. I have tried to tell you how -- what my perception was of this exceptional situation. I heard mention of Naser Oric ever since Belgrade, and what I heard and which was false but which was part of a legend that he was a former bodyguard of Milosevic, that he was part of the Yugoslav army, all kinds of things, and I knew nothing about. But I heard that he was someone who had military positions, elite positions, that he had the training of a fighter. And allegedly he spontaneously organised or led the resistance movement in Eastern Bosnia because he came from Potocari. Again, this is something that I heard and I don't know to this day whether this is true or not. But there were legends of this kind that were circulating. They were saying that Karadzic's mother was Albanian. You could hear stories that were of all kinds. And the image I had of Naser Oric was of someone who, on the basis of his military training, went to his native region to spontaneously organise the resistance against the Serbs. This was very important for me because it meant that he was something, he was atypical. Because in the rest of Bosnia, the resistance or the armed struggle against ethnic cleansing was organised under the guidance, strict guidance, of the Presidency in Sarajevo. You surely are aware of the exception close to Banja Luka of this enclave. I've forgotten the names now, but there was a Muslim leader who was an ally of the Serbs and who was later eliminated. So this was a situation that was relatively exceptional, at least at first glance. And on that basis, it was quite clear, and I tried to find out who I should negotiate with. And I considered Naser Oric as an emblematic figure. And upon arriving in Srebrenica, one might have found out that he had a religious background or something, and then I might have said that is the explanation. But for me, he was an emblematic figure. That is for certain. Whether he had power in the area, that is less certain, and I would be very prudent about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any questions? Judge Eser has got some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Very short questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I want to make sure that I have the indulgence of the interpreters and the technicians to go a few minutes beyond. I understand that we have got very few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just to be sure. You told us that you had been in Srebrenica before April 1993 two times, one in December. Can you clarify how long you have been in Srebrenica in December. You came there on the 4th of December?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Until the evening. We stayed there for three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Only for three hours?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Yes. With the convoy, which stayed there for three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And at the 11th of March, you stayed, if I'm correct, until the 14th of March. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: Until the 13th, I believe. From the 11th until the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, when you -- you told us you went to meet Dr. Mujkanovic in the Domavija Hotel, was this the only occasion when you met him or have there been other occasions? And if so, where you met him?

utterances.speaker: ERIC DACHY
utterances.text: That was the evening of the 11th of March. I met him in Domavija when we arrived. The next day on the 12th, I operated with him all morning and we spoke during the evening. The day after the 13th of March, we had some more consultations on the follow-up before leaving Srebrenica. And this was when we discussed fresh delivers of material and materiel to the enclave. I met him again once or twice. I met him in New York last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Dr. Dachy, on behalf of the Trial Chamber and on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and myself, I would like to thank you for having come over to give testimony in this case. You will be receiving all the assistance you require now from our staff. Madam Usher will usher you out of the courtroom. And if you require anything to facilitate your return back home at the earliest, please let me know. Once more, I thank you and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I thank you for the concern for the security of (redacted) on the ground, and I thank you for intervention in that connection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.text: I should say that obviously the witness for tomorrow wasn't scheduled for tomorrow, it was this witness, and it's really just that he arrived last night and we're able to proof him this afternoon and tomorrow morning so we're happy to bring him tomorrow afternoon if that's all right with the Prosecution.
